solutions.explanation:
Assume \(P\ne0\), \(s/P>0\), \(1+k>0\), and \(k\ne0\). These conditions allow a unique real logarithmic solution. First isolate the power containing \(n\):
\[
(1+k)^n=\frac{s}{P}.
\]
Taking common logarithms and using the power rule gives
\[
n\log(1+k)=\log\left(\frac{s}{P}\right).
\]
Since \(k\ne0\), we have \(\log(1+k)\ne0\), so
\[
n=\frac{\log(s/P)}{\log(1+k)}.
\]
All these steps are reversible under the stated assumptions, establishing choice \(\text{A}\) in that case.

The assumptions matter. For a positive base, if \(k=0\), the original equation reduces to \(P=s\), so either every real \(n\) works or none does. If \(k\ne0\) and \(P=0\), every real \(n\) works when \(s=0\), and none works otherwise. If \(k\ne0\), \(P\ne0\), and \(s/P\le0\), there is no real solution because \((1+k)^n\) is positive.

In particular, \(k=0\) and \(P=s=1\) give every real \(n\), while the proposed quotient is \(0/0\). Thus \(\boxed{\text{A}}\) is the conditional formula, but no unique answer is guaranteed as written.
solutions.title: Isolate the power and take logarithms
